newsitem.title: GERMANY: Italy's Prodi says Germany lacks commitment to EMU.
newsitem.headline: Italy's Prodi says Germany lacks commitment to EMU.

text.p: Italian Prime Minister Romano Prodi on Monday accused Germany of lacking political commitment to the European Union's planned single currency, saying Rome was making more effort to tackle its problems than Bonn.

Laying down the law to a German public which is openly sceptical about whether Italy's track record is strong enough to allow it into monetary union, Prodi said Italy, in contrast to Germany, was at least fully in favour of the currency plan.
"We see our future in Europe. I don't know if that is the case in Germany," he told a news briefing in Frankfurt.
Falling short of criticising German Chancellor Helmut Kohl by name, Prodi added: "Last year Germany was a model. This year Germany is a disaster...I would expect stronger leadership from Germany."

Earlier, Prodi lashed out at Germany's political leadership for failing to take the action needed to shape up the German economy for a punctual start of monetary union in 1999 by cutting its budget deficits and lowering public debt.
Prodi told Reuters Financial Television, "There is a difference between Italy and Germany. We have economic problems and I have prepared a strategy to solve them."

Germany, posting its highest unemployment level since the 1930s, has run into trouble as the government focuses on saving to meet the political goal of currency union rather than tackling economic problems, such as high unemployment.
Long-delayed and much-needed reforms of its tax and pension systems have been proposed, but are still politically deadlocked within the consensus-driven German decision process.
"Germany has more political problems than economic problems," Prodi said, adding: "If Germany wanted it could exercise the political leadership which is needed now."
The visit to Germany was Prodi's second in 11 days. He met Bavarian premier Edmund Stoiber in Munich and top industrialists and bankers in the financial capital, Frankfurt.
He also held private talks with Hans Tietmeyer, president of Germany's central bank, the Bundesbank.
Stoiber has been one of the most vocal politicians in Germany in insisting that the future euro currency must be rock-solid.
For most Germans, this means excluding countries such as Italy and Spain -- which have been better known for conducting inflationary policies than for their emphasis on stability.

Tietmyer has also been sceptical in the past about whether Mediterranean countries have the track record to ensure a stable single currency. He declined to make any substantial comment on his talks with the Italian premier.
Prodi, in his comments to reporters, emphasised Italy would be ready to join EU's currency union in 1999 and expected to be allowed in.
"It is puzzling to me that every other day some one is authorised to say Italy/Spain should not come in. That is difficult to understand," he said.

This year will be critical for nations wishing to join the currency union in 1999 as it will be their last chance to show that budget deficit and government debt ratios meet the strict Maastricht Treaty entry criteria set down in 1991.

Political leaders will choose the first group of nations to adopt the new currency early next year, and it is largely expected to include Germany along with France, the Netherlands, Belgium and Luxembourg as well as a few others.
Prodi said markets were already honouring Italy's efforts to ensure it, too, qualified on merit.
"Look at my record for the past and my plans for the future. I am organising consistent policies and the markets perceive this," he said.
